opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a few reasons. When we started thinking about agents, there was a lot of excitement around transactional tasks, like booking a flight, ordering food, filling out a form. Those are really compelling demos, but when we looked at where people actually spend time, a lot of knowledge work is really about finding information, reading a lot of sources, and pulling it together into something useful. That felt like a place where a model could add a lot of value, maybe even more than saving someone a few clicks on a checkout page.

The second reason was about risk and trust. With transactional actions, if the model makes a mistake, it actually does something in the world. It buys the wrong thing or sends the wrong email, and that's harder to undo. With synthesis, the output is a report the user reads. They can check the citations, decide what to trust, and the cost of a mistake is much lower. That made it a better first problem while we were still learning how these agents behave over long horizons.

And third, it was a capability we thought was necessary for the bigger vision anyway. If you want an agent that eventually does complex tasks for you, it first has to be really good at researching, browsing, reasoning over what it finds, and knowing when it has enough information. Deep Research was a way to push hard on those core skills, and with reinforcement learning on browsing and reasoning tasks, we saw the model get much better at things like backtracking, changing its search strategy, and digging into obscure sources.

So it wasn't that we thought transactional stuff doesn't matter. We think the two will come together eventually. Synthesis just felt like the most valuable and tractable place to start.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes research and synthesis as foundational agent capabilities, but does not say they are prerequisites for making new scientific discoveries.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it came down to where we thought the model's capabilities were actually strong enough to be useful, and where the cost of being wrong was something a user could tolerate.

With research, if the model goes and reads a hundred sources and synthesizes them into a report, the user can look at that output. They can check the citations, they can see the reasoning, and if something's off, they haven't lost anything except a little time. Whereas with transactional stuff, like booking a flight or making a purchase, the stakes are completely different. If the model gets it wrong, you've actually bought the wrong ticket. So the bar for reliability is much higher, and you also need a lot more infrastructure around permissions and confirmations and guardrails before you'd want to ship that broadly.

The other piece is that we were really excited about reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, and research is an almost perfect setting for that. The model has to plan, browse, read, backtrack when it hits a dead end, and keep going for a long time without losing track of the goal. You can set up training where the model learns to do that end to end, and the thing it's getting better at, finding and combining information, is genuinely valuable on its own. Like, a huge fraction of knowledge work is basically this. People spend hours pulling together information from a bunch of places and trying to make sense of it.

And I'd say the capabilities you build for research transfer. Browsing well, reading carefully, knowing when you've found enough and when you haven't, those are all things you need for more action-oriented agents too. So it wasn't that we didn't care about actions, it was more that synthesis felt like the right first step, where the model could already be really good and where people would actually trust the output.

r001.rationale: The response says that a huge fraction of knowledge work involves gathering information from many places and making sense of it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses research synthesis and its value, but does not present synthesis as a prerequisite for making new scientific discoveries.

astra-6.text: We wanted to focus on helping people make sense of complex questions. Often, the hard part isn’t taking an action; it’s gathering the relevant information, reconciling conflicting sources, and figuring out what it all means for your situation. Information synthesis felt like a useful foundation: give someone a well-supported understanding of a problem so they can decide what to do next. Transactional actions introduce another set of challenges around permissions and the consequences of getting something wrong.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to focus on a task where the model could do a lot of useful work autonomously, but the user could still review the result before acting on it. With research, it can spend time searching, reading, and synthesizing information, then give you a report with citations so you can check its conclusions. Transactional actions introduce additional challenges around permissions and consequences. Information synthesis felt like a valuable place to start: doing the time-consuming work of bringing sources together and helping someone understand a question more deeply.
